chapter_note.about: Combinational circuits have no memory: the outputs depend only on the inputs right now. This chapter covers the building blocks GATE keeps asking about: decoders, multiplexers (and how to wire one to realise a function), adders, universal gates, and the timing of a circuit. Most questions reduce to two moves. Either write each gate's output as a set of minterms, or count lines, gates and delays with powers of two. In the examples, A' means NOT A.
chapter_note.simple: A combinational circuit is a box of switches with no memory, so its output is decided only by what you feed in right now. A decoder lights exactly one lamp out of many. A multiplexer is a railway points switch that picks one of many inputs. An adder does school addition one column at a time, and it can be sped up by working out all the carries together. You can build every gate out of just NAND gates. A circuit is only as fast as its longest chain of gates. In exam words: decoders, multiplexers, adders with ripple or look-ahead carry, universal gates, and propagation delay with hazards.

cards.title: Decoder
cards.simple: Think of a hotel lobby with a row of 8 room lights and a keypad. You type a room number in binary, and only that room's light turns on. A decoder is that keypad-to-lights box. With 3 input wires you can name 8 different rooms. Every other light stays off. Big decoders can be built by stacking small ones, like a lobby with a floor button first and a room button second. In exam words: an n-to-2ⁿ decoder has n inputs and 2ⁿ outputs, and exactly one output (a minterm) is 1 for each input combination.
cards.idea: A **decoder** reads a binary number on its inputs and raises exactly one output line, the line with that number. n inputs give 2ⁿ outputs. Each output is one minterm of the inputs.
cards.definition:
An n-to-2ⁿ decoder has inputs $x_{n-1}\dots x_0$ and outputs $D_0\dots D_{2^n-1}$.

$D_i = 1$ exactly when the input number equals $i$, so $D_i$ is minterm $m_i$.

- $n$ = number of input lines, $2^n$ = number of output lines.
- With an enable $E$: $D_i = E\cdot m_i$.
- A' means NOT A (also written $\bar A$).
cards.intuition_full: A decoder is a truth table turned into hardware. Each output is an AND gate wired to recognise one input pattern, so the output is 1 for that pattern and 0 for all the others. That is why every output is a minterm and why any Boolean function can be built by OR-ing the right outputs. The count 2ⁿ comes from the number of different patterns n bits can make. A bigger decoder can be built from smaller ones with enable inputs. The first decoder uses the top bits and its output enables exactly one of the second-layer decoders, which use the low bits. Memory chips use the same idea: the high address bits pick the chip and the low bits pick the byte inside it.

examples.setup: A 3-to-8 decoder has inputs A, B, C (A is the most significant bit). The inputs are A=1, B=0, C=1. Which output is 1?
steps: The decoder has 3 inputs, so it has 2³ = 8 outputs D0 to D7. Exactly one of them will be 1.
Read ABC = 101 as a binary number: 4 + 0 + 1 = 5.
Output D5 goes to 1. The other seven outputs stay 0.
D5 is the AND of A, B' and C, written D5 = A·B'·C. That is minterm m5, the one row of the truth table where ABC = 101.
Add an enable input E. With E = 0 every output is 0, even for ABC = 101, so D5 drops back to 0.
examples.answer: D5 = 1 and the rest are 0. A decoder turns a binary number into one active line.

examples.setup: A 32 KB memory is built from eight 4 KB chips. The CPU puts the 15-bit address 0x2B7F on the bus. A 3-to-8 decoder on the top address bits picks the chip. Which chip is selected, and what is the offset inside it?
steps: 32 KB = 2¹⁵ bytes, so the address has 15 bits. A 4 KB chip holds 2¹² bytes, so it needs 12 address bits. That leaves 15 − 12 = 3 bits for the decoder.
0x2B7F = 0010 1011 0111 1111 in binary. As a 15-bit address that is 010 | 1011 0111 1111.
The decoder input is the top 3 bits, 010 = 2, so output D2 is 1 and chip 2 is selected.
The offset inside the chip is the low 12 bits, 0xB7F = 2943.

examples.setup: Many real decoders have active-low outputs: the selected output is 0 and all others are 1. What does a 3-to-8 active-low decoder output for ABC = 101?
steps: The selected line is still D5, because 101 = 5.
Active-low means 'asserted' is 0. So D5 = 0 and D0, D1, D2, D3, D4, D6, D7 are all 1.
Each output is now the NAND of the three literals instead of the AND: D5' = (A·B'·C)'.
examples.answer: Outputs D7 down to D0 read 11011111. The number of the low output is still 5.

cards.why: Decoders turn an address into a single select line, which is how memory and registers are chosen. In GATE: count decoder inputs and outputs, or build a bigger decoder from smaller ones.
how: Count the lines: n inputs give 2ⁿ outputs, and 2ⁿ items need n inputs.
Read the input bits as a binary number to find which output is high.
For a bigger decoder, give the high bits to a first decoder whose outputs enable the second layer.
Count the chips: one first-layer decoder plus one second-layer decoder per enable line.
cards.mistake: Forgetting the first-layer decoder when building a large decoder from small ones. A 4-to-16 decoder from 2-to-4 decoders needs 4 second-layer decoders and 1 more to enable them, so 5 in all.
edge_cases: With enable E = 0 every output is 0, whatever the inputs are.
A decoder with n inputs always has exactly one output high (when enabled), never two.
Each output is one minterm, so ORing outputs builds any function (card c7).
Active-low decoders flip every output; the number of the selected line does not change.
connections: Foundations: **Binary** (found.binary) gives the binary place values used to read the input number.
A decoder with enable is the building block for memory chip selection (coa.memory).
Decoder outputs are minterms, so they connect to the minterm sets in card c7.

cards.title: Multiplexer basics
cards.simple: A multiplexer is a railway points switch for signals. Many tracks come in, one track goes out, and a small control lever decides which incoming track connects to the exit. The lever is a binary number. With 3 lever wires you can pick any of 8 tracks, because 3 bits give 8 numbers. Whatever is on the chosen track appears at the exit. In exam words: a 2ⁿ-to-1 multiplexer has n select lines, and the select number picks which data input appears at the output.
cards.idea: A **multiplexer (mux)** passes exactly one of its data inputs to the single output. The **select lines** hold the binary number of the input to pass. 2ⁿ data inputs need n select lines.
cards.definition:
$$Y=\sum_{i=0}^{2^n-1} m_i(S)\cdot I_i$$

- $I_i$ = data input number $i$.
- $S$ = the select lines $S_{n-1}\dots S_0$, and $m_i(S)$ is 1 only when $S$ equals $i$.
- For a 2-to-1 mux: $Y=S'\cdot I_0+S\cdot I_1$.
cards.intuition_full: A multiplexer is a decoder plus a row of AND gates plus one OR gate. The decoder turns the select number into one active line. Each active line enables exactly one AND gate, which lets one data input through, and the OR gate collects the single survivor. So the equation is a sum of products, but only one product can be non-zero at a time. That is why the select lines count is log₂ of the data inputs. The reverse device, a demultiplexer, sends one input to one of many outputs. A mux is also the standard way to build a bus: many registers connect to the data inputs, and the select picks which register drives the bus.

examples.setup: An 8-to-1 multiplexer has data inputs I0 to I7 = 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0. The select lines are S2 S1 S0 = 1 1 0. What is the output Y?
steps: 8 data inputs need log₂ 8 = 3 select lines, S2 S1 S0. The select lines carry the number of the input to pass.
Read S2 S1 S0 = 110 as binary: 4 + 2 + 0 = 6.
The mux connects input I6 to the output. Every other input is ignored.
As an equation, Y is the sum of (select pattern × input). Only the term for 110 is non-zero: Y = S2·S1·S0'·I6 = 1·1·1·1 = 1.
examples.answer: Y = 1. A multiplexer copies one chosen input to the output.

examples.setup: A 32-bit datapath chooses the ALU input from one of 8 sources (registers or constants), using one multiplexer per bit. How many multiplexers are needed, and how many select lines does each have?
steps: Each bit of the 32-bit value is chosen independently, so each bit needs its own 8-to-1 mux.
Number of muxes = 32, one per bit.
Each mux has 8 data inputs, so it needs log₂ 8 = 3 select lines.
All 32 muxes share the same 3 select lines, because every bit takes its value from the same source.
examples.answer: 32 muxes of 8-to-1, each with 3 select lines, and the 3 lines are common to all of them.

examples.setup: A register file has 48 registers and one read port. How many select lines does the read multiplexer need, and how many select codes are never used?
steps: 48 is not a power of two. We need the smallest n with 2ⁿ ≥ 48.
2⁵ = 32 is too small and 2⁶ = 64 is enough, so n = 6.
The select lines can name 64 inputs, but only 48 exist: 64 − 48 = 16 select codes are unused.
examples.answer: 6 select lines. Rounding down to 5 would leave 16 registers unreachable.

cards.why: Multiplexers choose between data sources and are the engine behind buses, register files and ALU input selection. In GATE: count the select lines, read the output for given selects, or build a function with a mux (cards c3 and c4).
how: Count the data inputs N and take n = ⌈log₂ N⌉ for the select lines.
Read the select lines as a binary number, with S₀ as the least significant bit.
The output equals the data input with that number.
For a wide bus, use one mux per bit and share the select lines.
cards.mistake: Reading the select bits in the wrong order, or counting data inputs from 1 instead of 0. With S1 S0 = 10 the output is I2, the third input, not I1.
edge_cases: The select number is read with the first select line as the most significant bit unless the question says otherwise.
If the number of inputs is not a power of two, round the select lines up and leave some codes unused.
A 2-to-1 mux needs only one select line: Y = S'·I0 + S·I1.
If two data inputs carry the same signal, the select lines between them make no difference.
connections: A decoder (card c1) is the select half of a multiplexer.
Functions with a mux (card c3) feed constants and literals into the data inputs.
Mux trees (card c4) combine small muxes into big ones.

cards.title: Functions with a multiplexer
cards.simple: Say you have a rule with three yes/no questions, A, B and C, and a big switchboard. You let A and B pick a row on the switchboard. Each row then only has to answer a much smaller question about C: always yes, always no, same as C, or opposite of C. The switchboard is the multiplexer, and filling in each row is easy. This trick lets one multiplexer replace a pile of logic gates. In exam words: use n−1 variables as select lines, and set each data input to 0, 1, x or x' by comparing the two truth-table rows that share the same select value (Shannon expansion).
cards.idea: To build an n-variable function with a mux, put n−1 variables on the **select lines**. For each select value the function depends only on the last variable x. So each data input is just **0, 1, x or x'**.
cards.definition:
Shannon expansion on the last variable $x$:
$$F = x'\cdot F(x{=}0) + x\cdot F(x{=}1)$$

For each select value $s$ look at the pair $(F(s,0),\,F(s,1))$:

- $(0,0)\Rightarrow I_s=0$,  $(1,1)\Rightarrow I_s=1$
- $(0,1)\Rightarrow I_s=x$,  $(1,0)\Rightarrow I_s=x'$
cards.intuition_full: A mux with n select lines can hold any function of n variables: put the truth table values straight on the data inputs. That wastes half the mux. If you move the last variable x onto the data side, each select value only needs to describe how F reacts to x. There are only four possible reactions: F ignores x and is always 0, always 1, or F follows x, or F is the opposite of x. These are exactly the four inputs 0, 1, x and x'. So a 2ⁿ⁻¹-to-1 mux is enough for n variables, and at most one inverter is needed to make x'. The same idea works with any variable as the leftover one, as long as you pair the rows correctly: the two rows that differ only in the leftover variable. When the leftover variable is not the last in the table, take care to pair rows with the same remaining bits.

examples.setup: Realise F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,2,3,7) with a 4-to-1 multiplexer. Use A as S1 and B as S0. Find the data inputs I0 to I3.
steps: A and B go on the select lines. The data inputs are functions of the leftover variable C. The truth table rows pair up: the two rows with the same AB value differ only in C.
AB = 00 (rows m0, m1): F = 1 when C = 0 and F = 0 when C = 1, so F = C'. I0 = C'.
AB = 01 (rows m2, m3): F = 1 for both values of C, so I1 = 1.
AB = 10 (rows m4, m5): F = 0 for both values of C, so I2 = 0.
AB = 11 (rows m6, m7): F = 0 when C = 0 and F = 1 when C = 1, so I3 = C.
The data inputs are (I0, I1, I2, I3) = (C', 1, 0, C). Check row m7: AB = 11 selects I3 = C = 1, and F(7) = 1.
examples.answer: I0 = C', I1 = 1, I2 = 0, I3 = C. Each data input is one of 0, 1, C or C'.

examples.setup: F(A,B,C) = Σm(1,4,6,7). Use B as S1 and C as S0, with A on the data inputs. Find the data inputs I0 to I3.
steps: The selects are B and C, so the leftover variable is A. Pair the minterms that have the same BC but different A: BC = 00 pairs m0 (A=0) with m4 (A=1), BC = 01 pairs m1 with m5, BC = 10 pairs m2 with m6, BC = 11 pairs m3 with m7.
examples.answer: (I0, I1, I2, I3) = (A, A', A, A). Pairing m0 with m1 here would be wrong: the pairs differ in A, not C.

examples.setup: Realise X⊕Y (XOR) with a 4-to-1 mux and then with a 2-to-1 mux. Compare the data inputs.
steps: 4-to-1 mux, both variables on the selects: the data inputs are the truth-table values 0, 1, 1, 0. Only constants, no inverter.
2-to-1 mux, X on the select, Y on the data side: X = 0 gives X⊕Y = Y, so I0 = Y. X = 1 gives X⊕Y = Y', so I1 = Y'.
The smaller mux needs one inverter to make Y'.
examples.answer: 4-to-1: (0, 1, 1, 0). 2-to-1: (Y, Y'). A smaller mux trades size for one inverter.

cards.why: This is how GATE asks you to wire or read a mux circuit: it replaces a pile of gates with one multiplexer and a few constants. In GATE: find the data inputs for a given function, or find the function for given data inputs.
how: Choose the select variables (usually given) and name the leftover variable x.
List the minterm pairs: rows with the same select bits that differ only in x.
For each pair read (F at x=0, F at x=1) and write 0, 1, x or x'.
Check one or two rows by evaluating the mux for that input.
cards.mistake: Putting x and x' on the wrong inputs, which gives the complement of the function on that pair. Check a minterm: if F(m) = 1 and the leftover variable x = 1 in that row, the data input must be x or 1, never x'.
edge_cases: If F is the same for both values of x, the data input is a constant (0 or 1).
If every select value gives x or x', the function is XOR-like in x.
If the leftover variable is not the least significant bit, the paired minterms are not neighbours in the list.
With all n variables on the selects, every data input is a constant.
connections: Mux basics (card c2) explain the select and data inputs used here.
Mux trees (card c4) handle functions with more variables than one mux can take.
This is Shannon expansion, the same idea as splitting on a variable in logic and in decision diagrams.

cards.title: Mux trees and cascades
cards.simple: Imagine choosing one student out of 16 using a two-step process. First, each group of 4 students picks its own representative. Then the 4 representatives pick one winner. Each pick is done by a small 4-way switch. The low bits of the student number decide who represents each group, and the high bits decide which group wins. That is a mux tree. To read someone else's tree, replace each small switch by the signal it passes, starting from the one at the output. In exam words: a big multiplexer is a tree of smaller ones, the low select bits drive the first layer, and to analyse a cascade you collapse each mux into its output signal and work backwards from the final mux.
cards.idea: A large mux can be built as a **tree** of small muxes. The first layer takes the data inputs and uses the low select bits. Each later layer uses the next select bits. To analyse a cascade, **collapse** each mux to its output signal and work back from the final one.
cards.definition:
To build an $N$-to-1 mux from $k$-to-1 muxes:

- Layer 1 has $\lceil N/k\rceil$ muxes, layer 2 has $\lceil \lceil N/k\rceil/k\rceil$ muxes, and so on until one mux is left.
- Total muxes = sum of the layer counts.
- The select bits are $\log_2 N$ in total; each layer uses $\log_2 k$ of them, low bits first.
cards.intuition_full: A mux tree works like a tournament bracket. At each level a mux picks one signal out of its group, and the picked signals move up to the next level. The number of muxes in each layer is the number of groups. The select bits split the same way: the low bits say which input to take inside a group, the high bits say which group. The order matters. If you swap the select bits between layers, the same input number would reach a different input. To analyse a given cascade, you do not need the whole truth table. Each mux is just 'select ? this : that', so replace it by that expression, starting from the muxes whose inputs are plain variables or constants. If both inputs of a mux are the same constant, the mux collapses to that constant and its select line no longer matters.

examples.setup: Build a 16-to-1 multiplexer from 4-to-1 multiplexers. How many are needed, and how are the 4 select bits S3 S2 S1 S0 = 1011 routed?
steps: 16 inputs, 4 per mux: the first layer has 16 ÷ 4 = 4 muxes, M0 to M3. They give 4 outputs, and one more 4-to-1 mux M4 combines them. Total 4 + 1 = 5 muxes.
The low bits S1 S0 go to all four first-layer muxes. The high bits S3 S2 go to the final mux M4.
Take the select number 1011 = 11.
First layer: S1 S0 = 11, so every first-layer mux passes its input number 3: I3, I7, I11 and I15.
Final layer: S3 S2 = 10 = 2, so M4 picks the output of M2, which is I11. So Y = I11, the input numbered 11.
examples.answer: 5 multiplexers. The select number 1011 reaches input I11.

examples.setup: Three 2-to-1 muxes. M1 has select A and data inputs 0 (select 0) and 1 (select 1). M2 has select B and data inputs 1 (select 0) and 0 (select 1). M3 has select C, takes M1 on input 0 and M2 on input 1. For how many of the 8 combinations of A, B, C is the output Y = 1?
steps: Collapse M1: it passes 0 when A = 0 and 1 when A = 1, so M1 = A.
Collapse M2: it passes 1 when B = 0 and 0 when B = 1, so M2 = B'.
M3 selects M1 when C = 0 and M2 when C = 1, so Y = C'·A + C·B'.
C = 0: Y = A, which is 1 for A = 1 and any B: 2 combinations. C = 1: Y = B', which is 1 for B = 0 and any A: 2 combinations.
Total 2 + 2 = 4 combinations.
examples.answer: Y = 1 for 4 of the 8 input combinations.

examples.setup: A designer needs a 12-to-1 multiplexer and has only 4-to-1 muxes. How many are needed, and what changes compared with 16 inputs?
steps: Layer 1: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 muxes take all 12 inputs.
Layer 2: the 3 outputs need one more 4-to-1 mux, with one data input unused.
Total 3 + 1 = 4 muxes. The select code 11 on the final mux is never used.
examples.answer: 4 muxes. The unused code means the select number only ranges over 0 to 11.

cards.why: Real muxes come in fixed sizes, and GATE asks how many small muxes a bigger one needs or what a given cascade computes. In GATE: count the muxes in a tree, or find the output of a cascade.
how: Count the layers: divide the inputs by the mux size until one remains, rounding up.
Add the muxes in all layers for the total.
Give the low select bits to layer 1 and the next bits to the following layer.
To read a cascade, collapse each mux to its output signal and work back from the last mux.
cards.mistake: Forgetting the last mux in the tree, or sending the high select bits to the first layer. The first layer always uses the low bits.
edge_cases: If the input count is not a power of the mux size, the last layer has unused data inputs.
If both data inputs of a mux are the same constant, the mux output is that constant, whatever its select.
A tree of 2-to-1 muxes with N inputs always uses N − 1 muxes.
connections: Mux basics (card c2) give the single mux used at every node.
Functions with a mux (card c3) use a mux tree when a function has more variables than one mux can take.

cards.title: Half and full adders
cards.simple: Adding two single bits is like adding digits by hand. 1 + 1 = 2, but you can only write one digit, so you write 0 and carry the 1. A half adder does that for two bits: the sum bit says whether the bits are different, and the carry bit says whether both are 1. A full adder also takes the carry coming in from the right, so it adds three bits. You can build it from two half adders and one OR gate. In exam words: a half adder has S = A⊕B and C = A·B; a full adder has S = A⊕B⊕Cin and Cout = A·B + Cin·(A⊕B).
cards.idea: A **half adder** adds two bits: the sum is their XOR and the carry is their AND. A **full adder** also takes a carry-in, so it adds three bits. It is two half adders plus an OR gate.
cards.definition:
Half adder: $S=A\oplus B$, $C=A\cdot B$.

Full adder: $S=A\oplus B\oplus C_{in}$, $C_{out}=A\cdot B + C_{in}\cdot(A\oplus B)$.

- $\oplus$ = XOR (1 when the inputs differ).
- $C_{out}$ is 1 when at least two of the three inputs are 1.
cards.intuition_full: Count the ones among the three inputs. If the count is 0 or 2, the sum bit is 0. If it is 1 or 3, the sum bit is 1. That is the parity, and it is the XOR of all three. The carry is 1 when the count is 2 or 3: the majority. In the two-half-adder build, HA1 handles A and B. HA2 then adds the carry-in to HA1's sum. Two things can make a carry: A and B were both 1 (HA1 carries), or the partial sum and Cin were both 1 (HA2 carries). Both cannot happen together, since if A·B = 1 then A⊕B = 0. So an OR gate is enough to merge the two carries. The XOR gates are the slow ones, so the delay of a full adder is mostly two XOR delays on the sum path.

examples.setup: A full adder is built from two half adders and an OR gate. Add A = 1, B = 0 and carry-in Cin = 1. Find Sum and Cout.
steps: HA1 adds A and B: S1 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1 and C1 = 1·0 = 0.
HA2 adds S1 and Cin: S = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0 and C2 = 1·1 = 1.
The carry-out is the OR of the two half-adder carries: Cout = C1 + C2 = 0 + 1 = 1.
Cout S = 10 in binary, which is 2. Check: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2.
examples.answer: Sum = 0 and Cout = 1.

examples.setup: A 4-bit adder uses one half adder for bit 0 (no carry-in) and a full adder for each of bits 1 to 3. A half adder is one XOR and one AND. A full adder is two half adders and one OR. How many XOR, AND and OR gates are used?
steps: Half adder: 1 XOR, 1 AND, 0 OR. One of them: 1 XOR, 1 AND.
Full adder = 2 half adders + 1 OR: 2 XOR, 2 AND, 1 OR. Three of them: 6 XOR, 6 AND, 3 OR.
Totals: XOR = 1 + 6 = 7, AND = 1 + 6 = 7, OR = 3.
examples.answer: 7 XOR, 7 AND and 3 OR gates, 17 gates in all.

examples.setup: Check the full-adder carry formula against the majority rule for A = 0, B = 1, Cin = 1.
steps: Majority: AB + BCin + ACin = 0 + 1 + 0 = 1. Same result.
Sum: A⊕B⊕Cin = 0⊕1⊕1 = 0. Two ones, so the sum is 0 and the carry is 1.
examples.answer: Cout = 1 and Sum = 0. The carry formula and the majority rule agree on all 8 rows.

cards.title: Ripple and look-ahead carry
cards.simple: Picture four people passing a bucket of water down a line. Each person can only pass the bucket after receiving it, so a longer line takes longer. That is a ripple-carry adder: each bit waits for the carry from the bit before. A look-ahead adder is like a manager who looks at all the people at once and works out in advance who will hand over water. The answer arrives after a short fixed time, however long the line is. In exam words: ripple delay grows linearly with n; look-ahead computes every carry from G = AB, P = A⊕B and C0 with C(i+1) = Gi + Pi·Ci expanded, so its depth is constant for unlimited fan-in and Θ(log n) for fan-in 2.
cards.idea: In a **ripple-carry adder** every stage waits for the carry of the previous stage, so delay grows with the number of bits. A **look-ahead adder** computes every carry directly from the inputs using **generate** (G = A·B) and **propagate** (P = A⊕B).
cards.definition:
$$G_i=A_iB_i,\quad P_i=A_i\oplus B_i,\quad C_{i+1}=G_i+P_iC_i,\quad S_i=P_i\oplus C_i$$

Expanded: $C_1=G_0+P_0C_0$, $C_2=G_1+P_1G_0+P_1P_0C_0$, and so on.

- $G_i=1$: stage $i$ makes a carry on its own.
- $P_i=1$: stage $i$ passes an incoming carry on.
- Ripple delay is about $n$ stage delays. Look-ahead with fan-in 2 is $\Theta(\log n)$.
cards.intuition_full: A stage creates a carry in two ways. Either both of its bits are 1 (generate), or exactly one bit is 1 and a carry arrives (propagate). That gives C(i+1) = Gi + Pi·Ci. In a ripple adder you apply this one stage at a time, so C4 depends on C3, which depends on C2, which depends on C1. Look-ahead replaces Ci by its own formula again and again until only G, P and C0 are left. Each carry is then a two-level AND-OR of the inputs, and all carries are computed together. The price is more and bigger gates: the carry C_k needs terms with up to k+1 inputs. With gates of fan-in 2, combining n signals needs a tree of depth log₂ n. That is why GATE quotes Θ(n) for ripple and Θ(log n) for look-ahead.

examples.setup: Add A = 0111 and B = 0001 on a 4-bit ripple-carry adder. Each full adder passes its carry to the next stage 2 ns after its own carry-in arrives, and the first carry-in is ready at t = 0. Trace the carries and the delay.
steps: Stage 0 has A0 = 1, B0 = 1, Cin = 0. Sum 0, carry C1 = 1, ready at t = 2 ns.
Stage 1 (A1 = 1, B1 = 0) must wait for C1. Sum = 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 0, carry C2 = 1, ready at t = 4 ns.
Stage 2 (A2 = 1, B2 = 0) waits for C2. Sum 0, carry C3 = 1, ready at t = 6 ns.
Stage 3 (A3 = 0, B3 = 0) waits for C3. Sum 1, carry C4 = 0, ready at t = 8 ns. The result is 1000 = 8.
The carry crossed all 4 stages: 4 × 2 = 8 ns. A look-ahead adder forms G = A·B and P = A⊕B for every bit at once and then all carries in two more gate levels, so its delay does not grow with n.
examples.answer: Sum = 1000 (8) after 8 ns. The ripple delay is the number of stages times the carry delay.

examples.setup: In a carry look-ahead adder, expand C3 in terms of G, P and C0, and count the AND and OR gates in the two-level form (any fan-in).
steps: C3 = G2 + P2·C2, with C2 = G1 + P1·C1 and C1 = G0 + P0·C0. Substitute until only G, P and C0 remain.
AND gates are needed for the products with two or more literals: P2·G1, P2·P1·G0 and P2·P1·P0·C0, so 3 AND gates. The single term G2 needs no AND. One 4-input OR joins the four terms.
examples.answer: C3 = G2 + P2G1 + P2P1G0 + P2P1P0C0: 3 AND gates and 1 OR gate.

examples.setup: Does a ripple-carry adder always take n stage delays? Add 00000001 + 00000001 on an 8-bit ripple adder (2 ns per carry stage).
steps: Bit 0 has A0 = B0 = 1, so it generates a carry: sum 0, C1 = 1 at 2 ns.
Bit 1 has A1 = B1 = 0, so it kills the carry: 0 + 0 + 1 gives sum 1 and C2 = 0, whatever arrived.
From bit 2 on every stage sees carry-in 0 and nothing more ripples. The carries settle after about 2 stages, 4 ns, not 8 stages.
examples.answer: The delay depends on the data. The worst case needs the carry to propagate through every stage, for example A = 00000001 and B = 11111111.

cards.why: Carry delay is why adders are the slowest part of an ALU, and look-ahead is the standard cure. In GATE: ripple versus look-ahead delay, the gate count of a look-ahead carry, or the input that gives the worst-case ripple.
how: For ripple delay, multiply the number of stages by the carry delay per stage.
For look-ahead, write Gi = AiBi and Pi = Ai⊕Bi, then expand Ci+1 = Gi + PiCi.
Count gates: a product with two or more literals needs one AND, and each carry needs one OR.
Worst-case ripple: a carry generated at bit 0 that propagates through every higher bit.
cards.mistake: Counting the lone G term as an AND gate in a look-ahead carry, or adding a full-adder delay per bit for look-ahead. The G term is a plain wire, and look-ahead has a fixed number of gate levels.
edge_cases: If a stage has A = B = 0 it kills any incoming carry.
If a stage has A = B = 1 it generates a carry whatever arrives.
Using P = A + B (OR) instead of A⊕B gives the same carry but not the same sum.
A carry look-ahead block of 4 bits can be chained with ripple between blocks to limit gate size.
connections: Half and full adders (card c5) are the stages being chained.
In coa.alu the same carry lookahead idea is used to size and time the ALU adder.
The Θ(log n) bound is a fan-in-2 tree depth, the same counting as the mux tree in card c4.

cards.title: Circuit output as minterm sets
cards.simple: Think of each Boolean function as a guest list of the rows where the function is 1. An AND gate keeps only the people who are on both lists. An OR gate merges the lists. A NOT gate gives everyone who was left off. An XOR gate keeps people who are on exactly one list. So reading a circuit is just doing set operations, gate by gate, from the inputs to the output. In exam words: write each function as its set of minterms, then AND is intersection, OR is union, NOT is complement, and XOR is symmetric difference.

cards.intuition_full: A truth table is a column of 2ⁿ bits, and a gate acts on whole columns bit by bit. The minterm set is just the positions of the 1s in that column. So AND is the intersection of those sets, because both columns must have a 1 at the same position. The same reasoning gives union for OR and complement for NOT. XOR is 1 where the two columns differ, which is the symmetric difference. Working with sets avoids expanding algebra and is much faster than substituting values for every input row. A Π list is the same function seen from the other side: it names the rows where the output is 0, so the Σ set is everything else. cards.title: Universal gates and gate counts
cards.simple: Think of a NAND gate as a LEGO brick that fits everywhere. With only that one brick type you can build every other kind of gate, so a factory can stock a single part. A NOT is a NAND with its two inputs joined. An AND is a NAND followed by a NOT. An OR is two NOTs feeding a NAND. NOR is the same kind of brick the other way round. When an exam asks how many gates, you just count the bricks. In exam words: NAND and NOR are universal gates, any function can be built with only one of them, and gate counts must include inverters and share common sub-terms.
cards.idea: **NAND** alone (or **NOR** alone) can build every Boolean function, so they are called universal. NOT = NAND with joined inputs. AND = NAND then NOT. OR = NAND of the two complements.
cards.definition:
With NAND: $A'=(A\cdot A)'$, $AB=((AB)')'$, $A+B=(A'\cdot B')'$.

With NOR: $A'=(A+A)'$, $A+B=((A+B)')'$, $AB=(A'+B')'$.

Gate counts with NAND: NOT 1, AND 2, OR 3. With NOR: NOT 1, OR 2, AND 3.
cards.intuition_full: De Morgan's laws turn an OR into an AND of complements, and a NAND does 'AND then complement' in one step. So an OR needs the complements of A and B first, then one NAND. Each complement costs one NAND with joined inputs. That is where 3 comes from. A sum-of-products circuit is even cheaper in NAND form. If you replace every AND and the final OR by NAND gates, the two-level structure stays the same: NAND gates in the first layer, one NAND in the second. The inverters are absorbed by the bubbles. For multi-gate counts, look for a sub-term that two gates can share. Look for a sub-term that two later gates can share: counting it once is often how the minimum is reached.

examples.setup: Build F = A + B (OR) from 2-input NAND gates only, and trace it for A = 1, B = 0.
steps: Tie both inputs of a NAND together and it becomes a NOT: A' = NAND(A, A) = NAND(1, 1) = 0.
Do the same for B: B' = NAND(0, 0) = 1.
NAND the two complements: F = NAND(A', B') = NAND(0, 1) = 1. By De Morgan, (A'·B')' = A + B.
That is 3 NAND gates for one OR. A NOT takes 1 NAND, and an AND takes 2 (a NAND followed by a NOT-connected NAND).
examples.answer: F = 1 using 3 NAND gates. NAND gates can build NOT, AND and OR, so they are universal.

examples.setup: Build a 2-to-1 multiplexer Y = S'·A + S·B from 2-input NAND gates. How many NAND gates are needed? Trace S = 1, A = 0, B = 1.

N2 = NAND(S, B) = (S·B)'. For S = 1, B = 1: N2 = NAND(1, 1) = 0.
Y = NAND(N1, N2) = NAND(1, 0) = 1. This equals B, as a mux with S = 1 should give.
Gate count: S', N1, N2, Y = 4 NAND gates.
examples.answer: 4 NAND gates. The NAND-NAND structure turns the sum of products into NAND gates.

examples.setup: Build OR and AND from NOR gates only. Count the gates for each.

AND: complement each input with its own NOR: A' = NOR(A, A) and B' = NOR(B, B). Then NOR(A', B') = (A'+B')' = AB. That is 3 NOR gates.
With NAND it is the other way round: AND 2, OR 3.
examples.answer: OR takes 2 NOR gates and AND takes 3. NOR is cheap for OR, NAND is cheap for AND.

cards.title: Delay and hazards
cards.simple: Picture a relay race where several runners start at once on different tracks, and the next runner can only go when the slowest incoming runner has arrived. The finish time is set by the slowest chain of handovers, not by the sum of everyone's time. Gates work the same way: the delay of a circuit is the longest path from an input to the output. Sometimes two paths with different speeds disagree for a moment, and the output flickers wrongly for a short time. That flicker is called a hazard or glitch. In exam words: circuit delay is the longest path of gate delays, and unequal path delays can create a glitch such as X·X' pulsing to 1 after X rises.
cards.idea: The **delay** of a combinational circuit is the **longest path** of gate delays from an input to the output. At a gate with several inputs, wait for the slowest one. A **hazard** is a short wrong pulse on the output when paths of different delay disagree for a moment.
cards.definition:
Arrival time of a gate output: $t_{out}=\max(t_{in_1},t_{in_2},\dots)+d_{gate}$.

Circuit delay = the largest arrival time at the output.

A **static-1 hazard** is a brief 0 on an output that should stay 1. A **static-0 hazard** is a brief 1 on an output that should stay 0, as in $X\cdot X'$.
cards.intuition_full: Each gate needs a little time to react, so a change at an input spreads through the circuit like a wave. A gate cannot settle before its slowest input has settled, which is why you take the maximum at each gate and add the gate's own delay. The sum of all delays in the circuit is not the answer, because parallel branches work at the same time. Hazards come from the same fact. If one input of a gate changes now and another input, coming through a slower path, changes a little later, the gate briefly sees an inconsistent pair. In X·X', the NOT gate output lags behind X, so after X rises the AND gate sees X = 1 and X' = 1 for one NOT delay and produces a pulse of 1. Hazards matter only when the output is used as a clock or an asynchronous input.

examples.setup: Inputs A, B, C, D are ready at t = 0. G1 = AND(A,B) takes 3 ns, G2 = NOT(C) takes 1 ns, G3 = OR(G1,G2) takes 2 ns, G4 = XOR(G3,D) takes 4 ns and G5 = AND(G4,G2) takes 3 ns. G5 is the output. Find the circuit delay.
steps: All inputs are ready at t = 0. The circuit delay is the time until the output settles, so we follow the slowest path.
G1 settles at 0 + 3 = 3 ns and G2 at 0 + 1 = 1 ns. They work in parallel, so their delays do not add.
G3 waits for its slower input: max(3, 1) = 3. G3 settles at 3 + 2 = 5 ns.
G4 has inputs G3 (5 ns) and D (0 ns), so it starts at 5 and settles at 5 + 4 = 9 ns.
G5 has inputs G4 (9 ns) and G2 (1 ns), so it starts at 9 and settles at 9 + 3 = 12 ns. The critical path is A or B → G1 → G3 → G4 → G5.
examples.answer: The circuit delay is 12 ns, the length of the longest path.

examples.setup: Y = A·B + A'·C is built with a NOT gate (delay 2 ns), two AND gates (1 ns each) and an OR gate (1 ns). B = C = 1 and A falls from 1 to 0 at t = 0. Find the glitch on Y.
steps: Before t = 0, A = 1, so A·B = 1 and Y = 1.
A falls at t = 0. The AND gate A·B sees it and falls 1 ns later, at t = 1.
The NOT gate takes 2 ns, so A' rises at t = 2, and A'·C rises 1 ns later, at t = 3.
The OR gate adds 1 ns. It sees A·B = 0 from t = 1 and A'·C = 0 until t = 3, so Y = 0 for t = 2 and t = 3, then returns to 1 at t = 4.
Y drops for 2 ns although the Boolean value is 1 before and after. This is a static-1 hazard. Adding the consensus term B·C keeps Y at 1.
examples.answer: A 2 ns low glitch on Y. The extra term B·C removes the hazard.

examples.setup: The path delays in the first example are 3, 1, 2, 4 and 3 ns. A student adds all of them. Why is the answer wrong?

cards.title: Adder-subtractor and encoders
cards.simple: Subtracting is just adding the opposite number. To get the opposite of a binary number you flip all its bits and add 1. So one adder can both add and subtract if you put a flip switch on the B side: the same switch also supplies the extra 1 as the carry-in. A priority encoder is the reverse of a decoder. Many lines come in, and it reports the number of the highest line that is on, like a lift showing the top button pressed. In exam words: B XOR K with carry-in K makes an adder-subtractor (K=0 adds, K=1 subtracts); a priority encoder outputs the binary index of the highest asserted input plus a valid bit.
cards.idea: Put an XOR gate on every bit of B, and feed the control K to both the XOR gates and the adder's carry-in. **K = 0 adds, K = 1 subtracts** (A + B' + 1). A **priority encoder** outputs the number of the highest input that is 1.
cards.definition:
Adder-subtractor: $\text{result}=A+(B\oplus K)+K$, where $B\oplus K$ means each bit of $B$ XORed with $K$.

- $K=0$: $A+B$.  $K=1$: $A+\bar B+1=A-B$.

Priority encoder (4-to-2): outputs $Y_1Y_0$ = index of the highest $D_i=1$, and valid $V=D_3+D_2+D_1+D_0$.
cards.intuition_full: In two's complement, the negative of B is B' + 1. So A − B = A + B' + 1. An XOR gate with K = 1 flips the bit, and with K = 0 passes it through, so the XOR row is a controlled inverter. Using the same K as carry-in adds the +1 only when subtracting. The carry-out then means 'no borrow' for subtraction. An encoder works the other way round from a decoder. A plain encoder assumes only one input is high and ORs the codes of the high inputs. If two inputs are high, the OR of their codes points to a wrong third line. A priority encoder fixes this by ranking the inputs: higher inputs override lower ones. The valid bit tells you whether any input was high, because Y = 00 is otherwise ambiguous.

examples.setup: A 4-bit adder takes A and B XOR K, with carry-in K. Set K = 1 to subtract: A = 1001 (9) and B = 0100 (4). Find the 4-bit result and the carry-out. Then set K = 0.
steps: With K = 1 each bit of B is XORed with 1, so it is flipped: B = 0100 becomes 1011.
The carry-in of the adder is also K = 1. This adds the 1 that completes the two's complement of B.
The adder computes A + B' + 1 = 1001 + 1011 + 1 = 10101.
The 4-bit sum is 0101 = 5 and the carry-out is 1. So 9 − 4 = 5. (A carry-out of 1 means no borrow was needed.)
With K = 0 the XOR gates pass B unchanged and the carry-in is 0, so the adder computes A + B = 1001 + 0100 = 1101 = 13.
examples.answer: K = 1 gives 0101 = 5 (subtract). K = 0 gives 1101 = 13 (add).

examples.setup: A 4-to-2 priority encoder gives priority to the highest-numbered input. Inputs D3 D2 D1 D0 = 0011. Find Y1 Y0 and the valid bit V.
steps: D3 = 0 and D2 = 0, so they are ignored. The highest input that is 1 is D1.
D1 is input number 1, so Y1 Y0 = 01.
At least one input is high, so V = 1.
examples.answer: Y1 Y0 = 01 and V = 1. D0 is also high, but D1 has priority.

examples.setup: What goes wrong if a plain (non-priority) encoder sees D2 = 1 and D1 = 1 together, and what does a priority encoder do instead? What if all inputs are 0?
steps: The plain encoder ORs the codes: D1 gives 01 and D2 gives 10, so the output is 01 OR 10 = 11. That wrongly reports D3.
The priority encoder picks the higher input D2 and outputs 10.
With all inputs 0 the output is 00, the same as for D0 high. The valid bit V = 0 tells them apart.
examples.answer: The plain encoder gives 11 (wrong). The priority encoder gives 10. V = 0 marks 'no input'.

how: For the adder-subtractor, XOR every bit of B with K, then add A + (B⊕K) + K.
For K = 1 the result is A − B. The carry-out is 1 when no borrow occurred.
For a priority encoder, find the highest input that is 1 and write its number in binary.
Set V = 1 if any input is 1, else V = 0.
cards.mistake: Forgetting the carry-in K when using XOR to turn an adder into a subtractor. Without the +1 you get A + B' = A − B − 1, one too small.
edge_cases: With K = 0 the XOR gates pass B through and the circuit just adds.
The carry-out of a subtraction A − B is 1 when A ≥ B in unsigned values.
Signed overflow still needs the V flag check (see coa.alu).
A priority encoder with all inputs 0 gives Y = 00 and V = 0.
connections: Half and full adders (card c5) build the adder inside the subtractor.
Add/subtract and overflow (coa.alu) uses the same A + B' + 1 rule.

steps.caption: The decoder has 3 inputs, so it has 2³ = 8 outputs D0 to D7. Exactly one of them will be 1.
Read ABC = 101 as a binary number: 4 + 0 + 1 = 5.
Output D5 goes to 1. The other seven outputs stay 0.
D5 is the AND of A, B' and C, written D5 = A·B'·C. That is minterm m5, the one row of the truth table where ABC = 101.
Add an enable input E. With E = 0 every output is 0, even for ABC = 101, so D5 drops back to 0.
8 data inputs need log₂ 8 = 3 select lines, S2 S1 S0. The select lines carry the number of the input to pass.
Read S2 S1 S0 = 110 as binary: 4 + 2 + 0 = 6.
The mux connects input I6 to the output. Every other input is ignored.
As an equation, Y is the sum of (select pattern × input). Only the term for 110 is non-zero: Y = S2·S1·S0'·I6 = 1·1·1·1 = 1.

scenes.title: Function on a 4-to-1 mux: pair the rows

steps.caption: A and B go on the select lines. The data inputs are functions of the leftover variable C. The truth table rows pair up: the two rows with the same AB value differ only in C.
AB = 00 (rows m0, m1): F = 1 when C = 0 and F = 0 when C = 1, so F = C'. I0 = C'.
AB = 01 (rows m2, m3): F = 1 for both values of C, so I1 = 1.
AB = 10 (rows m4, m5): F = 0 for both values of C, so I2 = 0.
AB = 11 (rows m6, m7): F = 0 when C = 0 and F = 1 when C = 1, so I3 = C.
The data inputs are (I0, I1, I2, I3) = (C', 1, 0, C). Check row m7: AB = 11 selects I3 = C = 1, and F(7) = 1.
16 inputs, 4 per mux: the first layer has 16 ÷ 4 = 4 muxes, M0 to M3. They give 4 outputs, and one more 4-to-1 mux M4 combines them. Total 4 + 1 = 5 muxes.
The low bits S1 S0 go to all four first-layer muxes. The high bits S3 S2 go to the final mux M4.
Take the select number 1011 = 11.
First layer: S1 S0 = 11, so every first-layer mux passes its input number 3: I3, I7, I11 and I15.
Final layer: S3 S2 = 10 = 2, so M4 picks the output of M2, which is I11. So Y = I11, the input numbered 11.

scenes.title: Full adder from two half adders: 1 + 0 + 1

steps.caption: HA1 adds A and B: S1 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1 and C1 = 1·0 = 0.
HA2 adds S1 and Cin: S = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0 and C2 = 1·1 = 1.
The carry-out is the OR of the two half-adder carries: Cout = C1 + C2 = 0 + 1 = 1.
Cout S = 10 in binary, which is 2. Check: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2.

scenes.title: Ripple carry: the carry crosses every stage

objects.text: look-ahead: carries from G and P in 3 gate levels

steps.caption: Stage 0 has A0 = 1, B0 = 1, Cin = 0. Sum 0, carry C1 = 1, ready at t = 2 ns.
Stage 1 (A1 = 1, B1 = 0) must wait for C1. Sum = 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 0, carry C2 = 1, ready at t = 4 ns.
Stage 2 (A2 = 1, B2 = 0) waits for C2. Sum 0, carry C3 = 1, ready at t = 6 ns.
Stage 3 (A3 = 0, B3 = 0) waits for C3. Sum 1, carry C4 = 0, ready at t = 8 ns. The result is 1000 = 8.
The carry crossed all 4 stages: 4 × 2 = 8 ns. A look-ahead adder forms G = A·B and P = A⊕B for every bit at once and then all carries in two more gate levels, so its delay does not grow with n.

scenes.title: Gates as set operations on minterm rows

steps.caption: Write each function as a row of 8 slots, one per minterm 0 to 7. A 1 means the minterm is in the set.
G1 = f1 AND f2 keeps the minterms that are in both sets. f1 ∩ f2 = {1, 4, 6}.
G2 = G1 XOR f3 keeps minterms in exactly one of the two sets. Minterms 1 and 6 are in both, so they drop out. What is left is {4} from G1 and {2, 7} from f3: G2 = {2, 4, 7}.
Y = NOT G2 is the complement within 0 to 7: Y = {0, 1, 3, 5, 6}.
Y = Σm(0,1,3,5,6). The missing minterms 2, 4, 7 give the product-of-sums form Y = ΠM(2,4,7).

scenes.title: OR built from three NAND gates

steps.caption: Tie both inputs of a NAND together and it becomes a NOT: A' = NAND(A, A) = NAND(1, 1) = 0.
Do the same for B: B' = NAND(0, 0) = 1.
NAND the two complements: F = NAND(A', B') = NAND(0, 1) = 1. By De Morgan, (A'·B')' = A + B.
That is 3 NAND gates for one OR. A NOT takes 1 NAND, and an AND takes 2 (a NAND followed by a NOT-connected NAND).

scenes.title: Arrival times: the longest path sets the delay

steps.caption: All inputs are ready at t = 0. The circuit delay is the time until the output settles, so we follow the slowest path.
G1 settles at 0 + 3 = 3 ns and G2 at 0 + 1 = 1 ns. They work in parallel, so their delays do not add.
G3 waits for its slower input: max(3, 1) = 3. G3 settles at 3 + 2 = 5 ns.
G4 has inputs G3 (5 ns) and D (0 ns), so it starts at 5 and settles at 5 + 4 = 9 ns.
G5 has inputs G4 (9 ns) and G2 (1 ns), so it starts at 9 and settles at 9 + 3 = 12 ns. The critical path is A or B → G1 → G3 → G4 → G5.
